title: Arnstein v. Porter
lead: A composer’s improbable access allegations and circulated music produce a divided appellate decision over credibility and the two stages of copyright infringement.

actors.name: Ira B. Arnstein
actors.role: Composer demanding a jury and damages for alleged musical copying.

actors.name: Cole Porter
actors.role: Composer denying access and copying and seeking summary judgment.

actors.name: Judges Frank and Learned Hand
actors.role: Appellate majority requiring trial on remaining claims.

proceedings: The District Court accepted Porter’s denial and granted summary judgment on the deposition and recording record.
The Second Circuit changed specified noncopyright claims to jurisdictional dismissals.
It otherwise reversed and remanded, two to one, without finding infringement.
limits: The majority’s slightest-doubt language and deposition-rule discussion describe 1946 doctrine, not a present universal summary-judgment test. No plagiarism finding or damages award resulted.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Arnstein alleges access and copying, while Porter denies both
sections.cue: What evidence existed beyond the implausible portions of the story?
paragraphs: Composer Ira B. Arnstein’s music circulated through sales, distribution to radio stations, bandleaders and publishers, and public performances; more than a million copies of one composition had been sold. Arnstein contended that Cole Porter obtained access to his compositions and copied them. Porter denied both access and copying.

Arnstein sued Porter for musical copyright infringement, demanded a jury, and sought damages. Both were deposed and recordings were submitted. The district judge found some allegations about intermediaries or ‘stooges’ implausible, accepted Porter’s denial, and entered summary judgment. Porter also challenged copyright ownership, uncopyrighted material and titles, and alleged vexatiousness based on earlier unsuccessful litigation. The appeal to the Second Circuit thus involved both the factual infringement case and which components could remain.

sections.title: Frank separates copying from unlawful appropriation
sections.cue: Why could ordinary listeners and technical experts have different roles?
paragraphs: Judge Jerome Frank, joined by Judge Learned Hand, explained that copying could be admitted or inferred, usually from access plus similarity. Without other access proof, similarity needed to be striking enough to exclude independent creation. Technical comparison and experts could aid that inquiry.

Even copying did not necessarily infringe. Unlawful appropriation asked whether Porter took enough protected material appealing to ordinary popular-music listeners. A trained musician’s artistic taste could not substitute for that response, though appropriately directed expert testimony could help a jury understand audience reactions. Exceptionally striking similarity could establish both inquiries, but they remained distinct.

The majority listened to the music and found similarity insufficient alone to infer copying yet probative if access were established. It also could not call the resemblance necessarily too trivial to support appropriation. The access evidence therefore still mattered.

sources.pinpoint: Two copyright questions; 154 F.2d at 468–469,472–473 & nn.18–25

sections.title: The majority leaves credibility and live examination for trial
sections.cue: Did it prohibit summary judgment in every copyright case?
paragraphs: Applying the circuit’s historical caution where even slight factual doubt remained, Frank considered circulation and credibility unresolved. Implausible allegations did not authorize deciding Porter’s denial on depositions without live testimony. Trial cross-examination might yield admissions and permit demeanor assessment; prior deposition questioning did not necessarily exhaust it. The then-existing Rules 26 and 43 favored oral testimony when available, and the majority would not assume an exception allowing substitution in advance.

It nevertheless allowed summary judgment where documents, admissions, or unmistakably absent similarity made trial futile. Here it could not say a directed verdict necessarily would follow trial. Its appendix distinguished earlier defense victories resting on trial findings from present pretrial review, and compared a successful striking-similarity claim. Those authorities did not permit the appellate judges to decide these disputed facts themselves.

sources.pinpoint: Why trial required; 154 F.2d at 468–475 and appendix

sections.title: Some claims are excluded while the assigned-copyright claim survives
sections.cue: Why did earlier litigation not defeat every remaining claim?
paragraphs: The uncopyrighted Twilight Waltz and Duet from Song of David and the titles What Is Love and Night and Day were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. Titles lacked copyright protection, and the then-governing rules did not permit joining those nonfederal claims here.

Arnstein had assigned the copyright in A Mother’s Prayer but alleged an oral reversion agreement effective upon the now-deceased assignee’s death. With no party in that assignee’s chain before the court, the majority found the parol-evidence objection inapplicable; an earlier adverse ruling against someone else did not resolve this suit.

Prior losses likewise could not establish vexatiousness without res judicata prerequisites. Possible remedies for genuinely vexatious litigation differed from prejudging this action merely because its plaintiff had failed before.

sources.pinpoint: Claims excluded or restored; 154 F.2d at 474–475 & nn.30–34

sections.title: Clark sees no sufficient musical or access evidence
sections.cue: What is the precise divided disposition?
paragraphs: Judge Charles E. Clark would uphold dismissal. He heard no significant resemblance and favored intellectual score comparison alongside listening. Alleged copying involved commonplace short note sequences with different rhythms; his comparison of A Modern Messiah and Don’t Fence Me In found different meters and only five shared consecutive notes of different values.

Porter’s categorical denial and discovery without substantial counterproof made hoping cross-examination would create a case insufficient. Clark also disputed preemptive restrictions on deposition use and thought distance and absence rules should be applied to actual circumstances. Rule 56 contained neither a copyright exemption nor a slightest-doubt presumption; efficient testing was needed to prevent needless trial and settlement pressure after simplified pleading.

On February 11, 1946, the two-to-one panel modified the specified claims to jurisdictional dismissals and otherwise reversed and remanded. Arnstein obtained a trial opportunity on the remaining case, not a finding that Porter copied or unlawfully appropriated his music. Later editorial use of Clark’s writings should not be confused with this particular dissent.
